title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Sep 1, 2026
intro: This edition leans on measurement: Anthropic's own infra-noise and eval-methodology writeups quantify exactly how much slack your evaluation harness needs, two infrastructure wins cut inference cost hard (a 75% GPU bill drop, a cross-model KV-cache reuse trick), and two pieces cover keeping an increasingly autonomous coding agent contained.

cards.title: Give your agentic coding evals a resource floor and ceiling, not one pinned limit
cards.problem: Pinning a single container resource limit in an agentic coding eval conflates infrastructure failures with real model capability — Anthropic found configuration alone can swing scores past typical leaderboard gaps.
cards.apply: Specify two resource parameters per eval container instead of one: a guaranteed floor allocation and a separate, more generous hard-kill ceiling (e.g. 3x the floor), so a legitimate resource spike doesn't get killed and misread as a model failure.
cards.result: Anthropic reports infrastructure error rates fell from 5.8% under strict 1x enforcement to 2.1% with 3x headroom, while success scores stayed within noise (p = 0.40) — versus a 6-point swing on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (p < 0.01) between the most- and least-resourced configs.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-bench experiments measured infrastructure error rates and score variance across resource configurations.

cards.title: Turn on Claude Code's OS-level sandbox instead of trusting permission prompts alone
cards.problem: Permission prompts alone slow you down without stopping a subprocess a compromised or injected agent spawns from touching files or network destinations outside the current task.
cards.apply: Run `/sandbox` in Claude Code, then configure the filesystem allowlist and the network proxy's domain allowlist for your project — dual-layer isolation via Linux bubblewrap/macOS Seatbelt for the filesystem and a proxied Unix domain socket for network egress, both of which also cover spawned subprocesses and scripts, not just Claude's own tool calls.
cards.result: Anthropic reports sandboxing safely cuts permission prompts by 84% in internal usage, letting the agent run more autonomously while filesystem and network isolation still contain a compromised or injected process.

evidence.note: The 84% permission-prompt reduction is Anthropic's own reported internal usage figure.

cards.title: Use an agent-driven propose-train-test loop, with a monitoring agent, to close safety gaps faster than manual research
cards.problem: Manually researching and patching a model's alignment failures (deception, sycophancy, and similar) is slow, and each new checkpoint reopens the same work.
cards.apply: Set an agent loose on one alignment-failure category at a time with an iterative search-propose-train-test loop (literature search, propose a fix, train, evaluate), and add a separate monitoring agent that reviews every proposed method before it runs, to block capability degradation or fixes that just distill the target benchmark directly.
cards.result: Anthropic reports the approach closed 26-96% of the safety gap across 10 alignment-failure categories without degrading capabilities, generalized to withheld benchmarks and models up to 4.7x larger, and on a frontier checkpoint closed 65% of the safety gap in 60 hours — about 15,000x more efficient than Anthropic's production alignment procedure.

evidence.note: The safety-gap-closed percentages and efficiency multiplier are Anthropic's own measured benchmark results.

cards.title: Start agent evals at 20-50 tasks pulled from real failures, not a from-scratch test suite
cards.problem: Waiting to build a comprehensive eval suite before starting means agent regressions ship undetected for months, and a single grading method misses either objective correctness or subjective quality.
cards.apply: Convert 20-50 already-known production failures and manually-verified behaviors into your first eval tasks, written unambiguously enough that two domain experts grade them the same way; run each in an isolated, clean-state environment; and combine deterministic graders (unit tests, state checks) with an LLM-rubric grader for subjective dimensions, rereading real transcripts periodically to confirm the grader still measures what you think it does.
cards.result: Anthropic reports frontier models went from 40% to over 80% pass rate on SWE-bench Verified within a year of consistent eval-driven iteration, and that teams with evals adopt new models in days instead of weeks; tracking Pass^k (all k trials succeed) alongside Pass@k surfaces reliability gaps a single pass-rate number hides — a 75% per-trial success rate is only about 42% Pass^3.

evidence.note: The SWE-bench Verified trend and Pass^k math are Anthropic's own cited figures.

cards.title: Partition GPUs with NVIDIA MPS to run multiple model instances per card instead of one
cards.problem: A model-serving workload that only uses 15-20% of a GPU's compute per request still occupies the whole GPU when served one request at a time, wasting most of the card's capacity.
cards.apply: Enable NVIDIA CUDA MPS on your inference GPUs, set CUDA_MPS_ACTIVE_THREAD_PERCENTAGE to split each card into partitions (e.g. 4 instances at 25% SM each), map one model instance per partition, and combine it with dynamic batching. AWS notes the technique is model-agnostic for any encoder-decoder model served through Triton on NVIDIA GPUs, and works best when per-request GPU utilization is low and latency requirements rule out batching delays.
cards.result: AWS reports cutting infrastructure from 16 GPU instances to 4 for an ASR workload — a 75% cost reduction — while holding latency SLAs (mean under 650ms, p99 under 1,000ms) and reaching 92.1 requests/sec per GPU.

evidence.note: The GPU-count reduction, cost figure, and throughput/latency numbers are AWS's own reported deployment results.

cards.title: Move coding agents off developer laptops into isolated cloud sandboxes with a permission gateway
cards.problem: Coding agents running on developer laptops are resource-constrained, tied to one device, exposed to whatever credentials sit on that machine, and hard to monitor or run unattended in parallel.
cards.apply: Run each agent task in a short-lived micro-VM sandbox (e.g. Firecracker), route every tool call through a central gateway that enforces scoped permissions and logs all activity, and define tasks as YAML playbooks that combine agent-driven steps with deterministic code plus explicit validation and safety rules — triggerable from Slack, GitHub, cron, or CLI.
cards.result: DoorDash reports its Flux platform ran 130,000 engineering tasks and 25,000+ automated code reviews in a month across 300+ playbooks and 10,000+ weekly invocations, with a 95th-percentile end-to-end sandbox startup (VM boot, repo clone, tool install) under five seconds.

evidence.note: The task/review/playbook/invocation counts and sandbox-startup figure are DoorDash's own reported production numbers, relayed by InfoQ.

cards.title: Reuse another model's KV cache instead of recomputing prefill from scratch
cards.problem: Serving pipelines that pass the same context through multiple models (e.g. a small model then a larger one) redo the full prefill computation for each model even when an earlier model already processed that exact context.
cards.apply: Adopt a cross-model KV-cache translation layer that converts one model's cached key-value states into a form a different model can consume, instead of assuming cache reuse only works within a single model's own architecture.
cards.result: Researchers report prefill cost cut by up to 67% at 4K context length across model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B to Gemma-2-2B), and in a heterogeneous handoff (Llama3.1-70B to Qwen2.5-7B) latency dropped from 899ms to 138ms with accuracy close to native (44.0% vs. 45.7%).

evidence.note: Prefill-cost and latency figures are the paper's own benchmark results across within-family, cross-family, and heterogeneous model pairs.

cards.title: Filter MCP tool results in an extension hook before they reach the model, not after
cards.problem: An MCP tool can return output your agent shouldn't feed the model as-is — a leaked secret, or a payload large enough to blow the context budget — and by default that raw result goes straight into the conversation.
cards.apply: Use Codex's new extension hook that lets an extension inspect or replace an MCP tool's result before it reaches the model, and use it to redact sensitive fields or truncate/summarize oversized payloads at the boundary instead of downstream in the prompt.
cards.result: Tool output your agent shouldn't see raw — secrets, oversized payloads — gets filtered at the source instead of relying on the model to ignore or truncate it itself.

evidence.note: The release note only describes the hook's existence; the redaction/truncation use case is an editorial inference, not a measured or vendor-claimed result.
